evidence.claim: Mountain towns and a former toll road lead toward Mount Mitchell.
evidence.quote: Homesteads, farms, pastures, churches, and small communities dot the landscape in these rural areas of Yancey and Madison Counties.

evidence.claim: Mount Mitchell Scenic Drive links mountain towns, the South Toe River Valley and the Black Mountains.
evidence.quote: Eventually, the route will leave the Parkway and descend several thousand feet into the South Toe River Valley.

evidence.claim: The North Carolina Department of Transportation presents the byway as a journey through mountain scenery, recreation and Appalachian culture.
evidence.quote: Every mile of the Mount Mitchell Scenic Drive is packed with exceptional vistas of natural and geological sights, boundless recreation opportunities, and rare glimpses into Appalachian mountain culture and history.

evidence.claim: Its guide gives 52.5 miles and a driving time of one hour and 20 minutes.
evidence.quote: Total Distance: 52.5 Miles PA R. MT. MITCHELL B. Drive Time: 1 hr 20 min

evidence.claim: On NC 128, the two-lane summit road climbs in mild curves to a parking lot below the peak.
evidence.quote: The two-lane road has mild curves as it enters Mount Mitchell State Park.  It continues its ascent until it ends at the state park's parking lot, just below the summit of Mount Mitchell, the highest point in eastern North America.

evidence.claim: The South Toe drains the eastern slopes of the Black Mountains; farms, pastures and small communities occupy the rural stretches of Yancey and Madison counties.
evidence.quote: The South Toe River drains the eastern slopes of the Black Mountains

evidence.claim: That summit approach predates the scenic designation: a 1936 county map shows it as a toll road.
evidence.quote: The road itself existed earlier as a toll road on a 1936 county map.

evidence.claim: It received the number NC 128 on or around 1947.
evidence.quote: The current route was numbered NC 128, on or around 1947, as a new primary route and has remained unchanged since.

evidence.claim: In 2011, the Mount Mitchell Scenic Drive designation joined it with the Blue Ridge Parkway, NC 80 and US 19 and 19E in a corridor reaching I-26.
evidence.quote: Mount Mitchell Scenic Drive is an 52-mile (84 km) byway from the I-26 exit 9 to the top of Mount Mitchell, via US 19, US 19E, NC 80, Blue Ridge Parkway and NC 128.  This designation became official in 2011.

evidence.claim: Traveling toward the summit, start at I-26 Exit 9 and follow the corridor through Burnsville and Micaville.
evidence.quote: Mount Mitchell Scenic Drive is an 52-mile (84 km) byway from the I-26 exit 9 to the top of Mount Mitchell, via US 19, US 19E, NC 80, Blue Ridge Parkway and NC 128.

evidence.claim: Traveling toward the summit, start at I-26 Exit 9 and follow the corridor through Burnsville and Micaville.
evidence.quote: Mount Mitchell Micaville Burnsville

evidence.claim: Burnsville brings a town square and quilt blocks on barns and businesses at the west end of town.
evidence.quote: On the west end of town, colorful squares hanging on the sides of barns and businesses are part of the Quilt Trails of Western North Carolina.

evidence.claim: Beyond Micaville, NC 80 follows the South Toe before reaching the Parkway at Buck Creek Gap.
evidence.quote: It flows northward, alongside North Carolina Highway 80,

evidence.claim: Beyond Micaville, NC 80 follows the South Toe before reaching the Parkway at Buck Creek Gap.
evidence.quote: NC 80 connects with the Blue Ridge Parkway at the gap

evidence.claim: The Parkway and NC 128 complete the climb to the summit parking lot.
evidence.quote: The highway begins at mile marker 355 on the Blue Ridge Parkway

evidence.claim: A naval officer gives this mountain town its name: Captain Otway Burns, a hero of the War of 1812.
evidence.quote: it was named after Captain Otway Burns, a naval hero of the War of 1812.

evidence.claim: Burnsville was founded in 1834 on land conveyed by John "Yellow Jacket" Bailey.
evidence.quote: The town was founded on March 6, 1834, from land conveyed by John "Yellow Jacket" Bailey

evidence.claim: In 1909, Burns's grandson gave the town a statue, placed on a granite pedestal in the square.
evidence.quote: In 1909, a statue of Captain Burns was given to the town by his grandson, Walter Francis Burns Sr., and it was set on a granite pedestal in the center of the town square.

evidence.claim: Damage led to replacement of the original statue in the early 2000s.
evidence.quote: Due to damages, the original statue was replaced in the early 2000s.

evidence.claim: At the west end of town, quilt blocks on barns and businesses belong to the Quilt Trails of Western North Carolina; their patterns reflect the heritage of each location.
evidence.quote: On the west end of town, colorful squares hanging on the sides of barns and businesses are part of the Quilt Trails of Western North Carolina. Each block represents a different quilting pattern reflecting the heritage of the place in which it is located.

evidence.claim: Micaville takes its name from the mica mined here.
evidence.quote: The name comes from a mineral mined there called mica.

evidence.claim: In the early 1900s, the Black Mountain Railroad helped change an agricultural economy into a mining economy, with lumber harvesting added later.
evidence.quote: In the early 1900s, the Black Mountain Railroad, later operating as the Yancey Railroad (YAN) transformed the economy from an agricultural-based  into a mining community with later lumber harvesting adding into the economy.

evidence.claim: The line later operated as the Yancey Railroad.
evidence.quote: the Black Mountain Railroad, later operating as the Yancey Railroad (YAN)

evidence.claim: Its freight included mica and feldspar as well as fertilizer, building materials, livestock feed and steel spring wire.
evidence.quote: Micaville was a main point on the Yancey Railroad (YAN) carrying mica and feldspar, along with fertilizer, building materials, livestock feed and steel spring wire.

evidence.claim: Hurricane Agnes and flooding from other storms destroyed most of its bridges, track and branches.
evidence.quote: Due to  damage from Hurricane Agnes  and flooding from other storms most of the bridges, track and branches  were destroyed.

evidence.claim: NCDOT directs travelers to look for traces of old mining operations in town.
evidence.quote: Look for signs of old mining operations in the small unincorporated town of Micaville

evidence.claim: The area was known for the large sheets of mica extracted from its mines.
evidence.quote: the area is known for the huge ‘sheets’ of mica mined there.

evidence.claim: The road ends below the summit; a steep paved trail continues through conifer forest to the top.
evidence.quote: a parking lot where a steep paved 980-foot (300 m) trail leads through a conifer forest to the summit.

evidence.claim: Mount Mitchell reaches 6,684 feet, the highest peak east of the Mississippi in mainland North America.
evidence.quote: Mount Mitchell (Attakulla in Cherokee) is the highest peak of the Appalachian Mountains and the highest peak in mainland North America east of the Mississippi River.

evidence.claim: Mount Mitchell reaches 6,684 feet, the highest peak east of the Mississippi in mainland North America.
evidence.quote: Mount Mitchell's elevation is 6,684 feet

evidence.claim: Elisha Mitchell explored the Black Mountains in 1835 and determined that the range exceeded Mount Washington in New Hampshire.
evidence.quote: Elisha Mitchell, a professor at the University of North Carolina, who first explored the Black Mountain region in 1835. He determined that the height of the range exceeded by several hundred feet that of Mount Washington in New Hampshire.

evidence.claim: Returning to verify his measurements in 1857, he fell to his death at Mitchell Falls.
evidence.quote: Mitchell fell to his death at nearby Mitchell Falls in 1857, where he had returned to verify his earlier measurements.

evidence.claim: The summit observation deck opened in 2009, replacing a stone tower demolished in 2006.
evidence.quote: The 40-foot (12 m) stone observation tower on the summit was torn down in late 2006. A new observation deck was constructed and opened to visitors in January 2009.

evidence.claim: The summit trail measures 980 feet, continuing the journey beyond the parking lot on foot.
evidence.quote: a parking lot where a steep paved 980-foot (300 m) trail leads through a conifer forest to the summit.

evidence.claim: NCDOT prohibits tractor-trailers on the route and does not recommend it for recreational vehicles or buses.
evidence.quote: Tractor-trailer trucks are prohibited on this road and the route is not recommended for recreational vehicles or buses.

evidence.claim: When weather closes the Blue Ridge Parkway, access to NC 128 is cut off.
evidence.quote: If the Blue Ridge Parkway is closed due to inclement weather, access to NC 128 is cut-off.

flags: Driving order follows increasing strip-map miles, reversing the NCDOT guide and current draft: Burnsville, Micaville, Mount Mitchell.
The cache provides no construction campaign for the whole corridor; the road-history paragraph is limited to NC 128 and the 2011 byway designation.
The 2021 NCDOT guide predates Hurricane Helene. The cache does not establish present end-to-end access; the practical note is a cache check, not a live road-status check.
NCDOT gives 52.5 miles; the NC 128 article rounds the byway to 52 miles. The overview uses the guide.

The current draft's locomotive location is supported only by an undated secondary description and is omitted as an unverified present roadside feature. The pedestal inscription is omitted because its survival on the replacement monument is not established.
NCDOT's extracted historical account interleaves columns and calls the peak highest in the United States in 1844; that claim is not reused.
